newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani rupee seen steady against dollar.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani rupee seen steady against dollar.

text.p: The Pakistani rupee, unusually stable for the past few months, is under no pressure for an early depreciation, bankers said on Tuesday.

Plunging imports had depressed dollar demand, while foreign reserves were edging upwards, they said. Some argued that rising inflation and a strong dollar abroad had eroded the rupee's competitiveness against the yen, deutsche mark and sterling.

"Theoretically, the rupee can be devalued by at least one to two percent, but if imports are low and premiums in the kerb and interbank markets are down, the government can do without it quite easily," said the chief economist at a foreign bank, who asked not to be named.
"There seems no justification for a devaluation, at least in the near future," said Ijlal Alvi, treasury manager at Deutsche Bank, citing sluggish imports and a recent rise in reserves.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan has kept the rupee unchanged at 40.1200/40.3206 to the dollar since an October 22 devaluation. The rupee closed steady at 41.17 against the dollar in the kerb market on Monday.
The SBP sliced 17.14 percent off the rupee's dollar value in 1996, compared to 11.2 percent in 1995.
Liquid foreign reserves rose to $1 billion on March 1 from $850 million a week earlier. Consumer prices rose 13.4 percent year-on-year in January from 8.93 percent in January 1996.
Alvi said a high dollar supply in the kerb market, with only a small premium over the official rate, had reduced importers' demand for forward dollars from banks.
The recent stability of the rupee's official rate had also deterred speculation in the kerb, where dealers say many people sold dollars to invest in stocks that surged early this year.
The premium on six-month forward dollars has slipped to 7.5 percent from a peak of 10 percent a couple of months ago, dealers in the interbank forex market said.
They said the market believed the rupee would remain stable for another month or two. Even then, a depreciation of no more than one or two percent was expected.
"The premium on one-month forward dollars is currently around 3.5 to four percent and is likely to slip below three percent if the no-change perception continues," one dealer said.
Fahim Ahmad, forex analyst at Banque Indo-Suez, said a slump in imports was the main factor reducing dollar demand.
"Major pharmaceutical and auto companies have halted imports amid uncertainty about tariffs expected to be revised before or in the June budget," he said.

Only essential items such as petroleum products, edible oil and wheat were being imported while imports of chemicals, machinery and other capital goods and industrial raw material had fallen drastically, Ahmed said.
"One reason could be that economic activity has remained dormant in the past few months amid elections and most consumer goods manufacturers are sitting on huge inventories," he said.
